h1: Working as a brewer abroad: the skills that travel
title: Working as a Brewer Abroad | Craft Beer School
desc: Which brewing skills transfer between countries, what changes with local rules and climate. How to prepare before you move.
teaser: Brewing is a travelling trade, but not every skill packs into a suitcase. Know which ones do.
standfirst: Beer is made with the same biology everywhere. The rules, the water and the culture around it are not. This guide separates the two.
sections:
Yeast, malt and hops behave the same way in every country. A brewer who understands mashing, fermentation control and sanitation can work almost anywhere. Cleaning in place, careful records and calm troubleshooting are valued everywhere. So is sensory skill: tasting a tank and naming what is wrong.

Fluency in the numbers also travels: original and final gravity, bitterness units, dissolved oxygen, pH. Learn them in metric and in US units, since you will meet both.

Cleanliness habits are the same too. A brewer who sanitises everything that touches cold wort, whatever the country, earns trust in the first week. Documentation habits matter as well: a clear brew sheet means a colleague can take over mid-batch without guessing.

Rules differ widely. Licensing, food safety, labelling, excise and worker safety all change by country. Brewing terms and styles differ too. A bitter in one country is a pale ale in another. Local favourites and palates may differ from yours.

Check any qualification you hold against local expectations. A certificate recognised at home may mean little abroad. The reverse is also true.

Culture inside a brewery varies as well. Some are strictly hierarchical, others very flat. Watch first, then ask how things are done.

Water changes brewing more than almost anything. Some places have soft water, some hard. Desalinated or reverse osmosis water carries almost no calcium or magnesium, so brewers add salts to build a mineral profile. Altitude lowers the boiling point of water by about 1 °C for each 300 m, which changes hop extraction and evaporation in a boil.

Hot climates add a cold chain challenge for finished beer. Local grain differs as well: rice, maize, sorghum or cassava often feature in brewing in Africa and Asia. See a beginner's map of world beer styles for how regions differ.

Packaging differs by region. Some markets favour kegs and returnable bottles, others cans or large sharing bottles. Ask what the brewery fills and why.

Most countries require a work permit or visa for foreign workers. Rules change. Brewing may or may not be on a skills list. Contact the embassy or the national immigration service and read their current guidance. Never accept a job offer that asks you to work on a tourist visa.

Ask the employer what support they provide: permit sponsorship, housing, flights. Get everything in writing.

Keep copies of your qualifications, references and any translations an embassy might ask for. Check whether documents need an official stamp or a certified translation.
Learn the language of the brewhouse

Even in English-speaking countries, brewhouse slang differs. In non-English-speaking countries, learn the words for safety, cleaning chemicals, emergency stops and tank names, since confusion causes injuries. Learn a few phrases before you arrive and more on the job.

Safety standards also differ. Confined space entry, handling caustic soda and working with pressure vessels all have local rules. Take a local safety induction seriously.

Ask to see the safety data sheets for chemicals on site. A good employer will show them without fuss.

1. Gather evidence: batch records, course certificates and references.
  2. Write a CV that shows process knowledge and numbers.
  3. Research the market: styles, regulations and how breweries there are organised.
  4. Contact breweries directly and ask about short trial work.
  5. Plan your finances for a rocky first two months.

Read learning to brew while working full time if you are building skills first.

Join a local brewers' association or a homebrew club early. Contacts there open doors faster than job boards.

A broad grounding in the process gives you the vocabulary an employer will test in an interview. Brewing Fundamentals teaches the full process in metric and US units, with live questions from students in different countries.

We do not promise jobs. We do not quote salaries. Pay and conditions depend entirely on the country and the employer.

Be honest about what you do not know. A brewer who says I have not worked on this kit before, show me, gets better training than one who bluffs.
faqs: Can I work as a brewer in any country?
You need local work rights. Visa rules differ and change, so check with the relevant authority.
It depends on the country and the employer. Ask before you apply.
Sanitation, record keeping, troubleshooting, tasting and safe handling of chemicals and equipment.
Do I need to speak the local language?
Not always at first, but safety words matter from day one and fluency helps your career.
